title: The Kuleshov effect
hook: The same blank face looks hungry, sad or tender, depending on the next shot.
peek: A Soviet film teacher cut one expressionless close-up of an actor against different shots, and viewers praised the actor's range. The face never changed. The idea that editing can create the emotion became a founding lesson of film school.
lede: Around 1920, the Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov ran a simple experiment in editing. He took a close-up of the actor Ivan Mozzhukhin wearing a neutral expression and cut it against other images, such as a bowl of soup. Viewers, the story goes, saw hunger in one version and other feelings in the rest, and praised the subtle acting. It was the same shot every time.

bullets.text: Mozzhukhin was one of the best-known Russian stars of the day, which made the result more striking. Accounts of the other shots differ, but the most common version includes a bowl of soup and a little girl playing with a toy.
The original film has not survived. The main descriptions come from Kuleshov and his student Vsevolod Pudovkin, written down years later, so historians treat the exact details with some caution.

In a 1964 television interview, Alfred Hitchcock explained the idea using shots of himself. The same squinting smile looked kindly after a shot of a mother and baby, and rather less so after a woman in a bikini.

Later attempts to repeat the experiment have had mixed results. A 1992 study found little effect, while a 2016 study with modern viewers found the surrounding shots did nudge how people read a neutral face.
